The Common moorhen (Gallinula chloropus) is a widespread rallid inhabiting freshwater wetlands across Eurasia and Africa. Newly hatched chicks, emerging from eggs incubated at 36 °C [T = 36 °C], display a wet weight at birth of 13.9 grams [Wwb = 13.9 grams], a modest mass that reflects the semi-precocial developmental strategy characteristic of this species. This initial size is quickly offset by rapid growth under the intensive biparental care that moorhen chicks receive. The incubation parameters, derived from the classic study by Daws Whit 1999, indicate that the age at birth is 21.5 days [ab = 21.5 days], a period entirely consistent with the incubation durations recorded for other members of the family Rallidae at a temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C].

As the chicks develop, they undergo a predictable sequence of life-history transitions, most occurring under the elevated body temperatures typical of active homeothermy in this species (40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C]). The time since birth at fledging, marking the achievement of sustained flight and nutritional independence from parental provisioning, is recorded as 45 days since birth [tx = 45 days since birth] at a temperature of 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C]. This rapid transition to flight capability is an adaptive trait that reduces the nestling's vulnerability to terrestrial predators. Following fledging, the young birds enter a juvenile phase during which they continue to refine their foraging skills while remaining within the family territory. This period of somatic growth and behavioral development is critical for building the physiological reserves necessary for the upcoming maturation process.

Sexual maturation in the Common moorhen is attained relatively quickly after the fledging stage. Puberty, defined by the onset of gonadal activity, is reached at 135 days since birth [tp = 135 days since birth], a developmental milestone that synchronizes with the species' extended breeding season at a temperature of 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C]. However, first reproduction is not initiated immediately upon reaching physiological maturity. The time since birth at first brood, representing the age at which a female produces her first clutch of eggs, is deferred to 365 days since birth [tR = 365 days since birth], likely reflecting the energetic demands of territory acquisition and the establishment of a stable pair bond at a temperature of 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C]. This delay between physiological competence and actual breeding effort is a common life-history pattern among long-lived waterbirds.

The maximum longevity recorded for this species under natural conditions, measured at the same active metabolic temperature of 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C], is approximately 6789 days [am = approximately 6789 days], a duration that places the moorhen among the longer-lived members of the Rallidae relative to its body size. Adults that survive the high mortality of their first year can thus experience multiple breeding seasons, contributing to population stability. The ultimate total length measured from the tip of the bill to the end of the tail in fully grown individuals reaches 33.5 centimeters [Li = 33.5 centimeters], a size that reflects the species' robust, if somewhat compact, body plan suited for navigating dense emergent vegetation. The ultimate wet weight of a fully grown adult is 320 grams [Wwi = 320 grams], a value that exhibits some seasonal variation depending on fat deposition prior to migration or wintering.

Reproductive output in Common moorhen populations is structured around multiple nesting attempts per season. Females typically lay a clutch of 14 eggs per nest [N_R_i = 14 eggs per nest], a relatively large clutch size for a rallid of this body mass, and can produce approximately 14 broods per year [F_R_i = approximately 14 broods per year] under favorable conditions, though replacement clutches are common following predation events. This annual reproductive strategy provides a maximum production rate that ensures population recruitment despite significant nest predation pressure. The moorhen's ability to combine a moderately high fecundity per event with a long potential lifespan underscores its capacity to persist in dynamic wetland environments where breeding opportunities can be unpredictable.
